scenes.headline: How a chat model learns to read DNA
scenes.sub: Carbon-X: Qwen3-14B with six-base DNA words in its vocabulary.
scenes.say: Hi, I'm Gable! Carbon-X is a chat model you can paste raw DNA into, and it answers in plain English.

scenes.text: No separate DNA encoder. Carbon-X adds 6-base DNA words to the vocabulary, so DNA and English flow through the same decoder.
scenes.say: No separate DNA encoder. The language model just gets new words, six bases each, and one decoder learns both alphabets.

steps.say: A message arrives with a question and some DNA. The tokenizer tags any run of six or more bases.
English goes through the usual Qwen tokenizer. The DNA is cut into six-letter words.
Both look up rows in one embedding table. The DNA rows are new, and were trained first with the model frozen.
Then it is the ordinary Qwen decoder, and the answer comes back in English.

left.title: A substitution
left.say: Because the cuts are fixed every six bases, swapping one base changes exactly one token.

right.title: A one-base insertion
right.say: Insert one base and the frame shifts. Every later word becomes a different token.

items.say: First, only the new DNA embeddings learn.
Then three hundred billion tokens of genomes, biology and English, at a learning rate low enough to keep English.
Fine-tuning uses answers checked by code, not copied from a bigger model.
Last, reinforcement learning with rewards that code can verify.

scenes.title: Average of five DNA benchmarks
scenes.note: One sample per problem; two benchmarks built in-house
scenes.say: On five DNA benchmarks it averages sixty-six point seven, within noise of the best closed model, and ahead of every open model tested.

scenes.text: The tokenizer is the whole architectural change. A low learning rate and a long run did the rest.
scenes.say: So the trick is small. New words for DNA, then a long, gentle run that keeps English.
Six-base words, one decoder, three hundred billion tokens. And watch the reading frame.
